item.title: Along Himalayan Floods’ Path, Wiped Out Towns and Mounting Grief
item.description:
Taking a break from the noisy work of leading a school of over 500 students, Madhav Lamichhane would ride his motorbike down to the riverside Betrawati Bazaar every week. The principal skipped the busy shops around the town’s clock tower, preferring a quiet moment by the Ram temple to take in the “very beautiful flow” of the Trishuli River.

But on Aug. 26, as he was in school preparing for the first morning bell, the river below suddenly became a violent torrent that obliterated much of the town of Betrawati, erasing its square from the map. It left no trace of the temple, the market or the concrete bridges, and only fragments of the hundreds of homes that dotted either side of the river.

Mr. Lamichhane and the school, up on a hillside, escaped its wrath.

But about 200 students did not. The younger children, ages 5 to 11, had been waiting in the riverside town for a yellow school bus. The oldest, backpacks strapped on, had been slowly making their way uphill to the school when the deluge swallowed them.

“What can I say to the river?” Mr. Lamichhane sighed. He said that fewer than a third of the town’s families had scraped through without losing anyone, with many wiped out entirely.

“It was very beautiful previously,” he said. “It is a cultural and historical place, too. But all that became the past.”

When part of a Himalayan glacier near Nepal’s border with Tibet collapsed late last month, the ferocious water and debris that barreled through the gorge wiped out almost everything in their path for tens of miles. Two weeks later, the death toll stands at over 1,300, with 5,000 others missing, many most likely buried beneath the mud.

In the days after the floods, reporters from The New York Times traveled along the path of destruction, trying to reach areas cut off in a poor country with difficult terrain. What we found was towns and villages wiped off the map. Small reminders of life before remained in the sludge: a buried roof jutting out from the mud, a student’s backpack, an empty reading glasses case.

The dozens of bridges and the tens of miles of destroyed roads will surely be rebuilt. Technical assessments are already underway for a financing plan. The expected billions in costs will add to the debt of a small country still paying back loans it took to rebuild after a catastrophic earthquake just over a decade ago.

But helping to count the number of dead and telling the stories of wiped out communities is left to loved ones who were away at the time or who climbed to higher ground as the water closed in — now unsure whether to consider themselves lucky to have survived, or cursed to bear the crushing grief and loneliness.

The only lifeline connecting the remains of those settlements is a narrow dirt track that skirts the hills. The drive between some of the towns, which would have taken 15 minutes before the floods, took us seven to eight hours — the path was jammed with traffic and frequently blocked by mudslides caused by the last of the monsoon rains.

The Chilime hydropower tunnel, 10 miles from the border with China, was as far as we could get before the road collapsed into a dirt track along the river that was not safe to trek. Helicopters frequently flew through the narrow gorge on search and rescue operations to several tunnels in the area, where workers are feared trapped.

Officials who had flown into Syrabrubesi and Timure — the stretch beyond what was accessible by road — and survivors who were airlifted out said that hundreds of buildings had vanished, with nearly 1,000 people missing.

“The area is deserted now,” said Dolma Thangjen Sherpa, an elected member of the ward where Syabrubesi is, who was sheltering in a monastery in Kathmandu.

In the urban pockets along our journey — from Kathmandu to an army base and to a city nearly 100 miles downstream from where the floods originated that saw over 350 bodies wash up on its riverbanks — people flipped through lists of the dead, which ran multiple pages, and searched for clues in the lines of mangled bodies.

Most left in disappointment. Kami Delma Sherpa stared at a photograph of a woman with a golden tooth posted on the wall outside a hospital in Kathmandu, thinking she had finally found her sister, who worked at the border crossing. But when she went inside and looked at the body, it was not her.

As we traveled along the floods’ path of destruction, there were still small miracles to celebrate.

Kathmandu

A green house in Dhunge Bazaar remained standing, saving its residents, who had watched from their balcony as a whirlpool of mud and debris threatened to close in on them. A principal evacuated all of his students to safety, before his school was washed away. Three of the hundreds of workers trapped in hydropower project tunnels were pulled out alive more than a week after the floods.

Another unlikely escape was hiding in plain sight. We watched night fall over Betrawati last Friday, staring at a three-story house buried so deep in the sludge that only its roof and a sliver of its upper windows were visible. The search and rescue teams had moved on, the disposal of a decaying cow their last act that afternoon.

As we began our drive out of the ghost town late at night, we could hear only crickets and the roar of water. No one knew that a woman, Chandika Shrestha, was still clinging to life inside the house. Her family was among hundreds who had resigned themselves to their loss and had begun final ceremonial rites by cremating effigies of their loved ones.

The next day, locals heard a faint cry. Rescuers scrambled to dig her out.

But those kinds of miracles were few.

Betrawati, the site of a 1792 treaty that ended a war between Nepal’s kingdom and the Qing dynasty, laid bare the extent of the floods’ devastation.

What was once the town square, surrounded by lush paddy fields, now looks desolate — as if it had always been a riverbed, but the stream had shrunk. The two-story police station had been uprooted and deposited hundreds of feet away. A school bus with red seats was flipped on its side. Strewed around it were school bags, baby sandals, a broken speaker. A stench filled the air.

Pavitra Lamichhane, 32, took us to the riverbed to show where the house she had lived in with her 12-year-old son and mother-in-law once stood. She had been “going mad” searching for her son, her only hope, but they all survived.

With her husband, who died in a car accident two years ago, they had built a house in concrete to help it withstand earthquakes. But it was no match for the wall of mud from above.

“See that tree,” said Ms. Lamichhane, pointing to the ridge as her reference. “This should be the spot.”

Officials estimated that of a population of a little over 1,000 people, 315 people were lost in Betrawati. A large number of the survivors are homeless, sheltering on higher ground. In one hostel, aid workers prepared warm meals for 200 people. A generator hummed, powering mobile charging points for about 300 people.

The school where Mr. Lamichhane is principal had become the town’s relief hub, with trucks offloading aid material and social workers trying to console and entertain children uprooted from their homes.

On the morning of the floods, as Mr. Lamichhane was preparing for the day in his office, he got a call from the school bus driver saying he had heard of flooding upstream.

The driver had delivered two busloads of students to the school and was on his way to the town square for his final run.

“I scrolled on my mobile but did not see any news of the flood,” the principal said. He phoned a friend upriver, who told him the market had collapsed. “The flood is coming,” the friend exclaimed.

Mr. Lamichhane told staff to evacuate the 250 students already at the school to the forested areas above, while he and others rushed down toward the river to see what they could do.

He called anyone and everyone he could reach along the river: his staff who had not arrived at school yet, the parents of students.

Two phone calls, in particular, haunt him.

The first was to his elementary schoolteacher, whose riverside house he had often visited for a cup of tea. She had told him, “We are escaping! We are escaping!”

“The connection was lost,” he said. “She is among the missing.”

He remembers the second call, to another colleague, Ajay Kumar Yadav, with anger.

“I told him to come out. But he did not believe that the river could come up to there,” he said. “And he lost his life.”

As the principal spoke, he took his cap off to show his head, which he had shaved in a ritual performed to mourn dead relatives. (He lost two cousins who had been truck drivers along the border.)

Attendance had not yet been taken when the floods came, making identifying the missing students a challenge.

When we asked if he had to rely on families reporting their children as missing, he said, “There is no family to report,” adding, “The families are gone.”

Closer to the border with China, in the hillside village of Thulo Bharkhu, just before the road collapsed, a Buddhist monk held a vigil at his home for three members of his family — his son and two daughters-in-law — who were lost in the flood.

Singi Nurpu Lama is 80 and has difficulty walking. But he still went to other homes in the village to help lead their mourning prayers.

“There was flooding in the past also, but nothing like this,” the monk said.

One of the monk’s sons, Kshokyal Dorje Lama, was working in a bank in Kathmandu when he heard news of the flooding. He worried about his wife, Pratima Tamang, a nurse who was elected four years ago as the local municipality’s vice chairperson.

Mr. Lama tried to reach her on the phone, and the call went through.

“I felt like she was running, but I couldn’t hear anything,” he said. “Then the connection was lost.”

The couple had fallen in love when Ms. Tamang was still in nursing school and later married in a two-day ceremony in the village with over 1,000 guests. The houses were decorated with strings of lights. There was a feast of meat and rice and drinks. A large group of guests sang and performed a circle dance to celebrate.

Ms. Tamang could have gone abroad for better pay, as many Nepali nurses do. But she chose to go back to the village. The couple had planned to have their first child soon.

“I feel so alone,” he said. “Like fish without water.”

Maps by Pablo Robles.

item.title: Is A.I. Raising the Chances of Biological Warfare?
item.description:
Among the growing fears about artificial intelligence, one threat has proved particularly alarming: the possibility that A.I. could be used to create a new wave of biological weapons.

In April, biosecurity experts warned that it was disturbingly easy to get advice from chatbots about making pathogens more dangerous. In June, scientists and A.I. executives signed an open letter calling for new controls on the fabrication of DNA because A.I. can now speed up the design of toxins and viruses.

In August, scientists reported that they had used A.I. to build viruses not seen in nature. And on Thursday, Anthropic announced that it had blocked several attempts to use its models by people who might have been trying to weaponize pathogens.

Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic, followed up with a call on Saturday to slow down the development of A.I., with a set of proposals to keep it safe.

It would be wise, Dr. Amodei wrote, to ban “using AI for the production of biological weapons or allowing users to do so.”

These developments may give the impression that bad actors can now unleash previously unknown plagues on the world, all thanks to A.I.

But Drew Endy, a synthetic biologist at Stanford University who coauthored a report on biosecurity last year, said that current chatbots, like Anthropic’s Claude, don’t represent a sea change in the threat posed by biological weapons.

“In terms of the net impact on our biosecurity risk right now, I find it to be modest,” he said.

That could change, he added, as scientists develop A.I. models specializing in biological research.

Already these models can generate genomes for viable viruses not found in nature. It’s conceivable that the models may eventually be able to use those new genomes to create new weapons.

A biological weapon can be a virus or another pathogen, such as bacteria or fungi, that is designed to be unleashed against armies or civilians. Or it can take the form of toxins produced by organisms, such as botulinum from bacteria or ricin from castor plants.

(Biological weapons are distinct from chemical weapons, such as nerve gas, which scientists synthesize in labs.)

As far back as the Middle Ages, armies tried using disease as a weapon. In 1346, the Mongols loaded the bodies of people who died from bubonic plague onto catapults and launched them into the city of Caffa on the Black Sea.

Five centuries later, after scientists developed the germ theory of disease, those efforts became more precise. During World War I, German spies sneaked into the United States and other countries with vials of bacteria. They used it to kill thousands of horses and mules.

The Geneva Protocol prohibited biological warfare, but the great powers built biological weapons anyway. Eventually, the United States and the Soviet Union held gigantic stocks, from anthrax bombs to balloons loaded with wheat-killing fungi.

After signing the Biological Weapons Convention in 1975, the United States destroyed its massive stockpiles but continued studying biological weapons to develop defenses. The Soviet Union secretly carried out more investigations of pathogens, such as smallpox, for a new generation of biological weapons.

All of which is to say the threat of biological weapons was very real long before OpenAI and Anthropic appeared. And yet as far as is publicly known, biological weapons have caused very few deaths since World War II, for reasons that remain unclear.

“We don’t know what has been tried and failed, what has been deterred, what was too technologically challenging,” said Dr. Thomas Inglesby, the director of the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security.

That threat persists, Dr. Inglesby added, noting that someone trying to create biological weapons today can use powerful tools that previous generations could only dream of.

Synthesizing DNA has become fast and cheap, for example. In 2016, Canadian scientists reported that they had recreated horsepox, a virus related to smallpox that disappeared from nature in recent decades.

The scientists broke up the virus’s genome sequences into pieces, which they emailed to a DNA-fabricating company. The company sent the DNA molecules back to the scientists, who assembled them into a viral genome and inserted it into cells.

The infected cells then produced real horsepox viruses. At the time, this was hailed as a remarkable, if unnerving, feat. But advances in DNA synthesis and other technologies make such an exercise even cheaper and easier today.

Now chatbots might consult the scientific literature to answer questions that a biological weapons-maker would have. It’s a task at which A.I. can excel, Dr. Inglesby said, providing far more to bad actors than they could gather with simple web searches.

“It aims for the information to be usable,” he said of A.I. “It allows users to go back and forth infinite number of times to troubleshoot and explain in more detail, while providing just the right technical resources to back things up.”

Dr. Endy said he was glad to see that Anthropic was scanning queries for dangerous motives.

“If I take it face value, it appears that the team at Anthropic is trying to be a good citizen,” he said. “They have a new tool, and they’re trying to be responsible with it.”

The large language models that companies like Anthropic have built are trained on vast amounts of text, including the records of work by previous generations of scientists.

They may be able to retrieve that information quickly, or to find connections between previous findings that had gone overlooked. But they have no deep understanding of biology beyond what researchers have already discovered.

Other scientists, however, are building new A.I. models that can, to a certain extent, teach themselves biology. Instead of books and other texts, these models are trained on raw data about DNA and cells.

Scientists at Stanford University and the Arc Institute built one such model, called Evo2, which they trained on the DNA sequences of millions of species. Evo2 learned hidden patterns in genes, enabling the creation of new kinds of enzymes.

That led the scientists to wonder if they could make new genomes that could support life. The researchers put Evo2 through an additional round of training on genomes from one group of closely related viruses.

Known as microvirids, they are harmless to humans, only infecting the bacteria Escherichia coli. Evo2 offered up hundreds of thousands of new microvirid genomes, 16 of which gave rise to real viruses.

To safeguard Evo2, its creators have not trained it on viruses that infect humans or other related species. But in theory, such a version of Evo2 might be able to produce a variation on smallpox viruses.

Still, that would be no small task: the smallpox genome is 35 times bigger than the genomes of microvirid viruses. And even if all that effort paid off, it would only lead to a variation on a virus that was already turned into a biological weapon in the 1980s.

Still, Dr. Inglesby speculated that, without proper safeguards, programs like Evo2 could become more useful for making new biological weapons.

“With enough training data, these A.I. systems will be able to make predictions of more lethal, contagious, immune-evasive variants,” Dr. Inglesby said.

He worried that someday the models could come up with viruses that are not just variants, but are profoundly different from natural ones.

This week’s news from Anthropic raised more immediate concerns for biosecurity experts: The queries for information about influenza and other pathogens appear to have come from state-run labs, rather than lone biohackers.

“How a Ph.D. student can individually misuse a model for harm is only one small portion of the problem,” Dr. Inglesby said.

Dr. Endy worried that if governments start using A.I. for biowarfare research, they might help rekindle an arms race like the one during World War II.

“Today we live in a world where the U.S. State Department accuses North Korea and Russia of having programs, and suspects Iran and China,” he said. “And China accuses the United States and Russia. This is not something that was happening 10 years ago.”

Dr. Endy and Dr. Inglesby agreed that a lot could be done to reduce the risk of a catastrophe. Nations have negotiated biological weapons agreements in the past, and they can try to do so now.

The Biden administration put rules into place for DNA-synthesizing companies to screen orders for suspicious sequences. The Trump administration suspended them last year and has yet to issue new standards.

Dr. Endy argued that we have to do more than try to stop a biological weapon from being used. “We have to leapfrog ahead of that, and secure biology,” he said.

That means finding ways to defend ourselves from epidemics of all sorts, whether they’re engineered by humans or have jumped from animals into our species. Public spaces like hospitals and schools, he said, ought to be equipped with sensors that can detect airborne threats, for example.

“If I see an airborne virus in the space I’m in, I can act accordingly,” Dr. Endy said. “These biological risks are not magical.”

item.title: She Bashed the Government on a Private Call. Then She Was Detained for Months
item.description:
Until recently, Star Sabga spent her days making artisanal cheese and ranting about politics over the phone with her niece.

Ms. Sabga, 69, lived in a luxury seaside apartment in a suburb of Port of Spain, the capital of Trinidad and Tobago. Her niece, Genevievre Hadeed, and her niece’s husband, a bottled-water magnate named Dominic Hadeed, helped cover her costs.

But in June, that peaceful lifestyle was upended when police officers detained the Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga, accusing them of plotting to assassinate the prime minister.

The Hadeeds were held without charges for nearly a month, and Ms. Sabga for more than two months, under Trinidad’s state of emergency, a measure in place almost continuously since 2025 in response to rising violent crime, according to officials. The state of emergency allows authorities to carry out warrantless searches and detain people indefinitely without charges.

The detentions gripped the Caribbean nation, setting off a national debate about the government’s use of surveillance and preventive detention. The saga also exposed racial and political friction surrounding Trinidad’s Middle Eastern-descended minority, to which Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds belong.

Kamla Persad-Bissessar, the prime minister, did not respond to questions about the cases of Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds. But she defended the state of emergency, saying to reporters on Thursday, “It is very clear that the crime stats are down.” She added, “Maybe it’s not the best thing to do, but it was very successful.”

Governments around the region have increasingly turned to severe tactics in response to surging rates of violence. In El Salvador, more than 90,000 people have been detained, and nearly 500 have died in state custody, amid a four-year state of emergency, according to Amnesty International. Honduras and Jamaica have also used states of exception, during which certain rights are suspended amid an emergency, to the alarm of human rights groups.

Sandra Pellegrini, the Latin America regional team lead at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data, or A.C.L.E.D., a U.S.-based nonprofit organization that monitors conflict and protest data, has studied the use of emergency powers in the region. She said any reductions in crime have often been short-lived and come at the cost of civil liberties.

“Whether you’re a criminal or not, you’re still supposed to be able to access a fair trial,” she said, noting that protesters and government critics have at times become targets under law enforcement agencies with weakened restrictions.

Before his legal saga made headlines, Mr. Hadeed had been known as a critic of the administration. He criticized its tax policies in a public forum in March and objected to the government’s decision to cancel a lease for land his businesses had operated on since 2007. The Hadeeds were also known as prominent members of Trinidad’s Syrian-Lebanese minority group.

The nation is split almost evenly between Afro-Trinidadians, many of whom are descended from enslaved Africans, and Indo-Trinidadians, who trace their roots to indentured workers from India. Many people also have mixed heritage, and several prominent minority groups exist, including the Syrian-Lebanese.

Middle Eastern-descended Trinidadians have historically been associated with the People’s National Movement, currently the country’s main opposition party, and a notable number of successful businesspeople in the country are of Syrian-Lebanese descent, according to Sam Salloum, a Trinidadian businessman who is part of the community.

Politicians in the United National Congress, the governing party, frequently criticize the economic dominance of the Syrian-Lebanese community — often referred to as “the 1 percent” — and accuse them of political corruption and organized crime.

In June, the attorney general, John Jeremie, issued warnings to the ethnic minority during a motion to extend the nation’s state of emergency. He called them a “gang” that had “taken over” the opposition party.

Members of Parliament enthusiastically thumped their desks, punctuating Mr. Jeremie’s remarks.

Mr. Jeremie also confirmed that some Syrian-Lebanese people have had their U.S. visas revoked. He denied his government’s involvement in those decisions, but implied that U.S. intelligence agencies had flagged them for criminal ties. (The Hadeeds’ lawyer confirmed that their visas were among those that were revoked.)

Ms. Sabga read about Mr. Jeremie’s comments in the next day’s newspaper, according to court documents. Angry, she called her niece, Ms. Hadeed, to vent her frustration with how her community was being treated.

Less than two weeks later, just after dawn on June 24, the Hadeeds were startled awake when police officers, some with machine guns, swept into their home, according to affidavits by the Hadeeds. Officers declared they had a search warrant and seized electronic devices, including those of the Hadeeds’ three children.

It was not until Mr. Hadeed was separated from his wife and detained for multiple days that he was given a reason for the arrests: The Hadeeds were accused of plotting to assassinate the prime minister and other government leaders and of fostering ties to transnational crime.

Mr. Hadeed was “numb with shock, disbelief and horror,” he wrote in an affidavit denying the allegations. He later learned that Ms. Sabga, his wife’s aunt, had also been detained.

“The entire community was in shock,” said Mr. Salloum, who knew Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds. He said the community knew Ms. Sabga primarily for selling shanklish cheese, balls of fermented and strained yogurt covered in seeds and spices.

Mr. Salloum dismissed the idea that Ms. Sabga could be at the center of an assassination plot, saying she wouldn’t even spray a bug. “She gonna cry for the cockroach,” he said.

The Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga denied the accusations. Through their lawyer, they declined interviews.

In an affidavit, Mr. Hadeed said he suffered from medical conditions that were exacerbated in prison. Ms. Sabga and Ms. Hadeed were held in a women’s prison, where they said in affidavits that they were subjected to strip searches and filthy lodgings with no privacy, even to relieve themselves.

In the following weeks, court records revealed that a central piece of evidence in the case was a recording of the June 11 phone call between Ms. Sabga and Ms. Hadeed, which authorities had intercepted. To date, authorities have not explained why they had tapped the call in the first place, saying only in court documents that security agencies were specially trained to monitor “persons of interest.”

Roger Alexander, the homeland security minister, cited 13 written excerpts from Ms. Sabga’s impassioned conversation with her niece. Ms. Sabga used a slur against the prime minister, an Indo-Trinidadian woman, and called her “a target.”

“Somebody’s getting a bullet in their head,” Ms. Sabga had said. “What has to happen for this to cool down is the death of one of her members of Parliament.”

Mr. Alexander, who did not respond to requests for comment, wrote in a court document that those statements were part of “a developing plot or chatter pointing to threats to the life of persons in public life.” He said the authorities had worked with U.S. “partner agencies” and found that the Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga had connections to criminals, to whom they could “communicate deadly intent.”

The U.S. authorities, including the F.B.I., the Drug Enforcement Administration and the International Law Enforcement division of the Department of Justice, did not confirm or deny any criminal investigations involving the Hadeeds or Ms. Sabga.

The intelligence that authorities relied upon to detain the Hadeeds and Ms. Sabga was called into question when a local news outlet posted a leaked recording of the full 15-minute call in July. The recording showed Ms. Sabga had been privately venting her frustrations about what she saw as a political attack on her community, which she insisted was not involved in criminal activity.

The leak sparked intense and wide-ranging reactions.

Many condemned Ms. Sabga’s use of slurs against the prime minister, for which Ms. Sabga expressed regret in an affidavit — though she said her comments had been “wickedly twisted out of context.” Others saw the recording as discrediting the government’s claims of an assassination plot. The call did not involve Mr. Hadeed, raising questions about why the authorities detained him.

After a month in detention, the authorities released the Hadeeds and revoked their detention orders. A video on social media showed Mr. Hadeed returning to his office, hugging and kissing his employees and saying, “I missed you all.”

In July, Ms. Sabga was released from prison but was ordered to remain confined to her home. According to court documents, she was barred from leaving her apartment and her contact with family was severely restricted. In an affidavit, she described armed, camouflaged officers guarding her building.

On Thursday, more than two months after Ms. Sabga was detained, authorities released her from house arrest and revoked her detention order. On Friday, when local reporters asked Mr. Alexander about Ms. Sabga’s release, he compared her case to the search for the killer of Tupac Shakur, the American rapper.

“Tupac Shakur was shot in 1996, and the person was only charged this year,” he said, implying that the state’s investigation into Ms. Sabga would continue after her release. “It’s not over till it’s over,” he added.

The state of emergency is scheduled to expire this week, and hundreds of detainees are set to be released. Many, like Ms. Sabga and the Hadeeds, have not been charged with any crime.

item.title: Syrians Protest as Surge in Fuel Prices Adds to Cost-of-Living Crisis
item.description:
Syrians have taken to the streets to protest the government’s decision to raise fuel prices, a move that has added to the punishing cost of living in the country as it struggles to recover from a civil war that ended two years ago.

Over the past two days, Syrians in cities across the country have gathered in squares, blocked roads and set tires on fire, and called for the price increases to be canceled.

The protests began hours after the government announced on Sunday that it would temporarily raise prices for gasoline, diesel and other petroleum products as much as 40 percent. The energy ministry said the measures were necessary because of global shortages largely related to the U.S.-Israeli war with Iran and to a major overhaul at a refinery in Syria, which will reduce domestic refining capacity and increase the country’s reliance on imports.

The increases ranged from 9 percent for cooking gas to 25 percent for gasoline to 40 percent for diesel, the ministry said.

The explanations have done little to quell the anger.

In one video posted online, a man poured what he said was gasoline over his head and threatened to set himself on fire before a crowd intervened.

“We stood with you, please stand with us,” another man said in a different video posted from a protest, addressing President Ahmed al-Sharaa. “Some people are living off sugar and water.”

Syrians have dealt in recent months with soaring inflation on food and fuel. The price surges have stoked discontent with an interim government formed by the rebels who ousted President Bashar al-Assad in December 2024.

After the overthrowing of Mr. al-Assad ended a nearly 14-year civil war, Syrians hoped that a new government and the country’s reintegration into global markets would quickly improve the economy.

Those hopes have been repeatedly disappointed, with the situation becoming worse for many.

The Syrian government did away with subsidies on fuel and bread and has reopened its economy to international imports, which has contributed to rising prices.

Lingering U.S. sanctions have not helped, with the final restrictions lifted only last month.

Businesses and investors have also been wary of returning to the country. Major obstacles include uncertainty over the interim government’s fiscal policies and concerns about security.

Syria’s newly seated Parliament will hold a hearing Thursday with the energy minister, who is expected to discuss the higher prices.

Muhammad Haj Kadour and Reham Mourshed contributed reporting.

item.title: Saudi Leader Meets U.S. General as Widening Conflict Threatens Oil Markets
item.description:
Mohammed bin Salman, the Saudi crown prince and de facto ruler, met with the U.S. general who oversees the military’s Middle East operations on Monday as a lightning advance by Iranian-backed Houthi militants in Yemen threatened to unsettle global energy markets further.

A brief summary carried by Saudi state media said Prince Mohammed held talks with Adm. Brad Cooper, who leads the U.S. military’s Central Command, in the Saudi coastal city of Jeddah to discuss “the latest regional developments.” Central Command did not immediately comment.

Admiral Cooper began meeting with Saudi defense officials late last week to discuss intelligence sharing and munitions, according to two people familiar with his visit. They requested anonymity because they were not authorized to speak publicly.

Diplomacy between the Trump administration and Iran on ending the war has stalled. Instead, the regional conflict that began when the United States and Israel attacked Iran in February has widened, with a new front opening in Yemen between the Houthis and the internationally recognized government in Yemen that is backed by Saudi Arabia.

Last week, the Houthis, who rule much of northwestern Yemen, swept into the strategic port of Mokha on the Red Sea and also seized the island of Perim. Forces allied with the Yemeni government also withdrew from the Hunaish and Zuqar islands last week, according to Yemeni officials.

The Houthi advance has put Saudi Arabia, which has fought a long military campaign with the group, on edge.

Prince Mohammed spoke with President Trump about the escalation in Yemen last week and urged the United States to take military action against the Houthis, according to officials with knowledge of the conversations. Mr. Trump told him he was not willing to do so, the officials said.

The territorial gains have given the militants greater sway over the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a maritime choke point in the Red Sea.

Houthi officials have vowed to block Saudi shipping in the waterway, threatening another critical route for global oil shipments. Iran has effectively blockaded the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf since the U.S.-Israeli attack in late February, causing energy prices to soar.

The price of Brent crude, the global benchmark, jumped nearly 4 percent to over $108 a barrel, on Monday, reflecting investor worries over continued instability in the Middle East. The price of Brent is roughly 50 percent higher than before the war.

The renewed fighting has effectively reignited the Yemeni civil war, which had been largely quiet since a 2022 cease-fire. Saudi-aligned forces have attacked Houthi territory, while Houthi forces have repeatedly fired at sites in Saudi Arabia that they say are military and energy installations.

On Monday, the Saudi government’s civil defense issued alerts for the southern cities of Khamis Mushait and Abha, warning of incoming attacks. There were no reports of casualties.
